query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: At high temperatures, the wear resistance of thin-film FeNiCrCoCu coatings is primarily governed by the in situ formation of a dense, adherent oxide layer that limits direct metal-to-metal contact and reduces abrasive and adhesive wear.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu thin film on a conventional metal substrate with a typical nanocrystalline/metastable microstructure produced by sputtering or similar deposition.
generation.intervention: Expose the coating to a high-temperature wear environment (e.g., continuous sliding wear tests at elevated temperatures such as 500°C) while keeping the room temperature wear behavior as the baseline.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding or reciprocating wear tests under constant load in air, with temperatures sufficiently high to accelerate oxidation kinetics but below the melting point of the alloy (e.g., 450–600°C).
generation.structural_mediator: The oxide scale that forms on the coating surface (likely enriched in Cr-oxide components given the alloy composition) acting as a protective barrier.
generation.mechanism: When the coating is subjected to the elevated temperature, accelerated oxidation at the surface produces a continuous and adherent oxide layer. This layer increases the effective surface hardness and reduces direct metal contacts during sliding, thereby lowering friction and wear rates compared to the unoxidized (room temperature) state.
generation.predicted_outcome: In high-temperature wear tests, the coating will exhibit a lower wear rate and coefficient of friction relative to room temperature conditions; post-test microscopy and XRD will reveal a continuous, protective oxide film correlating with the improved wear performance.
generation.baseline: Wear behavior of the as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating at room temperature without significant protective oxide formation, where higher friction and wear rates are observed.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies under conditions where the temperature is high enough to enable sustained oxide formation (and not so high as to induce coating degradation or spallation) and with wear loads that allow the oxide film to function as a barrier. It might not be valid at temperatures too low for oxidation or too high where thermal stresses cause oxide spallation.
generation.uncertainty: The detailed chemistry and microstructural evolution of the oxide film (e.g., exact oxide phases and their adhesion characteristics) on FeNiCrCoCu are not fully characterized; thus, variability in oxide composition or differences in grain size and residual stresses may affect the protective behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings on a conventional metal substrate and subject them to controlled sliding wear tests at both room temperature and a high-temperature regime (e.g., 500°C) under identical loads and durations. Monitor the evolution of the surface by in situ or ex situ microscopy and XRD analysis to detect oxide formation.
measurements: Wear rate (volume loss per unit load and distance)
Surface characterization using SEM, EDS, and XRD to identify oxide phases and film continuity
Cross-sectional TEM analysis to assess oxide layer thickness and adhesion
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If high-temperature tests do not show the formation of a continuous, adherent oxide layer or if the wear resistance (in terms of lower wear rate and friction) is not significantly improved compared to room temperature, then the hypothesis – that the protective oxide layer governs the wear resistance – would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs), since their discovery by Yeh et al. in 2004, [1] have opened up researchers to a new alloy system that contains five or more equimolar principal elements. In equimolar HEAs, each element has an equal probability of occupying the lattice sites in a crystal structure such as face-centered cubic (FCC), [2] body-centered cubic (BCC), [3] or hexagonal structure [4] crystal structures. Lattice distortion, sluggish diffusion, high entropy, and cocktail effects have been identified as the core effects contributing to the superior properties, hardness, strength, ductility, erosion, tribocorrosion, corrosion, and oxidation/wear resistance [5] − [7] of HEAs in a wide range of temperatures over conventional alloys. Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 .
